doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Open-ended solos, Al the accordionist, and soloing for Mick on Miss You
summary: Ries compares freedom in his own gig with limits when playing with the Stones, where his solo on Miss You ends when Mick starts the verse. Al sat in on a Ukrainian polka.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you think you play differently when the length of your improvisation is open ended? Like last night you pretty much can decide as you’re playing how many choruses you’re going to do, where if you’re playing a solo with a band that — you’re not leading it, perhaps you know I need to limit myself. So is there a thought process that you take that into account? Like I’m going to do two choruses so do you play differently if you have a time limit?

Yes. I mean well for instance last night it was more open-ended and I didn’t have to limit, as you said, limit myself. I could do one, two, three or four or five. Like there was a period where that accordion player, Al, came up and sat in right. So now we’re incorporating a guy who does polka music with the accordion, because Ron Oswanski also is an amazing accordion player and can do the polkas, he grew up in a Polish household and he played all that stuff. But he also can improvise and play jazz, he’s incredible. So I called him and I said, “Are you going to bring your accordion?” He goes, “Well.” I said, “Well bring it, maybe we’ll do a duet.” And then before the gig he introduced me to Al. I said, “Well Al would you come and join us?” And I’m trying to © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

figure out what — so then we did this Ukrainian polka because of the Ukrainian situation. But Ron and I had done, I had to produce an album for Ron and we did that song on his record but we did it kind of like as a North African kind of vibe combined with this polka. So we tried to do that last night with Al but then on that I didn’t really improvise. I kind of let Al — which I played the melody with him and then just a little tiny solo, Ron would play a little solo, so just it was more about how do we feature, how do we make him like that’s his moment rather than my thing. It’s just like okay well we’re going to be part of your world now. So but yeah, I try not to worry too much about it. For instance like if I’m playing with the Rolling Stones I’m improvising every night on “Miss You” this famous song of theirs. But that solo is when Mick is out front in front of 50,000 people and he’s moving and dancing. So I’m watching when he takes the mic and starts the next verse, right? So my solo could be eight bars, it could be twelve, could be sixteen, could be — depending on his — so I’m actually just watching him thinking well sometimes occasionally I might go out a little bit too much jazz or whatever, but I try to really retain more of like I’m playing almost like rhythm guitarish things with a little bit of like — but I’m looking, okay my solo ends when he starts the verse. So I’m trying to like figure at the end of a phrase to like end so that he is comfortable starting. So then I’m really — it’s not so much about me soloing it’s about me playing these lines, riffing a little bit and then watching him move and then okay my solo is based on, and also because I love flamenco so a lot of the time when I’m playing with dancers I’m like watching the dancer and imitating the dance of flamenco that’s changing the way I play. So I don’t mind that. I don’t feel it’s limiting. I feel it’s — that’s the conversation.
